text:
SaveChanges interceptors

A SaveChangesInterceptor can run around the high-level SaveChanges() call. EF Core docs describe interceptors as allowing interception of both low-level database operations such as commands and higher-level operations such as calls to SaveChanges.

Conceptually:
SavingChanges     before EF saves
SavedChanges      after EF believes SaveChanges succeeded
SaveChangesFailed if SaveChanges fails

If SaveChanges succeeds, then a "saved successfully" interceptor can run even if the outer transaction later rolls back.
code: await context.SaveChangesAsync();

text:
Command interceptors

Command interceptors are lower-level. They run when EF creates/executes database commands. If SaveChanges sends an INSERT, command interceptors can run for that INSERT.

If the outer transaction later rolls back, the command interceptor already ran because the command really was executed.

Conceptually:
SaveChanges
  command interceptor sees INSERT
  database executes INSERT inside transaction
  EF receives generated values
  SaveChanges interceptor runs
later:
  transaction rollback

Because from EF's point of view:

SaveChanges succeeded.
The later transaction rollback is a separate operation.

Example: begin a transaction, add order, SaveChanges reports success, then RollbackAsync rolls the row back, but SaveChanges itself already succeeded.

theme: Command interceptor may not run when no SQL command is sent
text:
But if EF fails before sending any command, then command interceptors for database commands may not run.

Example:
SavingChanges interceptor runs
DetectChanges runs
validation/model/client-side issue happens
no SQL command is sent
command interceptor does not see INSERT
SaveChangesFailed runs

theme: Rule: SaveChanges vs command interceptor scope
text:
So the rule is:

SaveChanges interceptor: tied to SaveChanges lifecycle.
Command interceptor: tied to actual database command execution.
Rollback later does not undo the fact that interceptors already ran.
That is one reason audit/event publishing inside SaveChanges can be dangerous when using manual transactions. The save may succeed but the transaction may later roll back.
Generated value example: identity / auto-increment key. SQL Server uses IDENTITY by convention for int key.
Generated value example: database sequence used as a default value.
Generated value example: database default constant.
code:
entity.Property(o => o.Status)
    .HasMaxLength(30)
    .HasDefaultValue("Pending")
    .ValueGeneratedOnAdd();

text:
Sequences can be part of database generation, but there are two slightly different cases:

Database-generated value:
  The database creates/returns the value as part of INSERT/UPDATE.

Client/generated-by-provider value:
  EF/provider creates the value before sending SQL, or fetches a sequence value before the INSERT.

Both can result in "after SaveChanges, my entity has a value." But they are not all generated at the exact same moment.

theme: Generated value: database default SQL expression
text: Generated value example: database default SQL expression.

theme: SQL Server OUTPUT pseudo-tables for generated values
text:
Is there a special generated pseudo-table?

No. There is no separate SQL Server pseudo-table called generated.

The usual SQL Server options are:

OUTPUT INSERTED.SomeColumn
for values after INSERT or UPDATE

OUTPUT DELETED.SomeColumn
for values before DELETE or before an UPDATE.

Truly database-generated during INSERT/UPDATE

These are generated by the database when the SQL runs:
identity columns
default constraints
computed columns
rowversion
sequence defaults like NEXT VALUE FOR ...
trigger-generated columns

Example:
INSERT INTO Orders (...) VALUES (...);
SELECT generated columns back;

EF can then populate the tracked entity with the returned values.
Generated value example: computed column.
Generated value example: trigger-generated value. EF must be told that the property is generated.

theme: Need generated ID before the next step
text:
1. You need database-generated IDs before the next step

Very common.

Example:
Begin a transaction, create an Order, add it, SaveChanges so order.Id exists, then create a Payment with OrderId = order.Id, add it, SaveChanges, commit.

Database-generated values are available through INSERTED in SQL Server's OUTPUT clause.

For an INSERT, INSERTED represents the row after SQL Server has applied generated values, such as:
IDENTITY values
rowversion values
DEFAULT constraint values
computed column values
Generated value example: updated-at column generated on insert/update. Exact behavior usually needs a trigger or computed column. HasDefaultValueSql handles insert; a trigger can handle update.

EF/provider-generated before INSERT

These are values EF or the provider may create before sending the command:
GUID primary keys
sequential GUIDs for SQL Server
some custom ValueGenerator values
HiLo values, after EF has fetched a block from a database sequence

For example, SQL Server GUID key values can be generated client-side by the provider. They are "value generation", but not always "the INSERT returned this value."

theme: Parent-child relationship can usually be inserted in one SaveChanges
text:
Example order with Lines collection, adding two OrderLine values and calling SaveChanges once.

EF can insert the order, get its ID, and insert the lines in the same flush.

Do not call SaveChanges early just because there is a parent-child relationship; EF usually handles that.
Generated value example: SQL Server rowversion / timestamp.
code:
entity.Property(o => o.RowVersion)
    .IsRowVersion();

text:
For SQL Server provider, a non-primary-key Guid property configured with ValueGeneratedOnAdd() can still get a client-side generated GUID from EF Core.

Example:
entity.Property(o => o.PublicId)
    .ValueGeneratedOnAdd();

Meaning: when a new entity is added, this property should get a value.

theme: When generated ID needed outside EF relationship fix-up
text:
EF can often handle parent/child inserts in one SaveChanges. But sometimes the next step needs the generated ID outside EF's relationship fix-up:
call external API
write audit message
insert into table not mapped by EF
use order.Id in raw SQL
create files with ID in filename

Then you may need an intermediate save.
Generated value example: client/provider generated GUID. For SQL Server, Guid keys configured generated-on-add can be generated client-side as sequential GUIDs by the provider.
code:
entity.Property(o => o.PublicId)
    .ValueGeneratedOnAdd();

text: For SQL Server, EF Core uses its sequential GUID generator for Guid columns configured as generated-on-add. Microsoft's docs say this is automatic for GUID primary keys, and for non-key properties you can configure the same behavior with ValueGeneratedOnAdd(). The SequentialGuidValueGenerator docs also state it is the default generator for SQL Server Guid columns set to generated on add.

theme: Large import as one giant SaveChanges is bad
text:
2. You are importing a large file in chunks

Imagine importing 500,000 rows.

Bad idea: add every mapped row to the same context and call one SaveChanges at the end.

Problems:
huge change tracker
high memory usage
slow DetectChanges
very large SQL batch
harder error isolation

The practical compromise: chunked SaveChanges()

For many inserts, a common EF pattern is to begin a transaction and save chunks.
code: await using var tx = await context.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();

theme: SaveChanges per object is usually worse
text:
Then why not call SaveChanges() after every object?

Because that is usually even worse.

Bad pattern: inside foreach, add one product and await SaveChangesAsync for each row.

3. Huge SQL batches

EF cannot always send everything as one efficient command. It may need to split commands because of:
SQL parameter limits
provider batch size limits
identity/generated key handling
foreign key dependency ordering
command timeout risk
large transaction log growth

So one massive SaveChanges can become a lot of database work in one big burst.

What about performance?

Roughly:
SaveChanges per row: simplest mentally, usually worst performance
One huge SaveChanges: fewer flushes, but high memory/change-tracker cost
Chunked SaveChanges: usually practical for large imports
Real bulk API: fastest for very large imports

For very large inserts, EF Core may not be the best tool. You may use:
SqlBulkCopy
PostgreSQL COPY
raw SQL
table-valued parameters
bulk extension libraries
staging tables
Chunked import pattern: begin one transaction; for each chunk, project rows into Product entities, AddRange, SaveChanges, then ChangeTracker.Clear; commit or rollback.

theme: Harder failure recovery with one huge save
text:
4. Harder failure recovery

If item 89,431 fails because of bad data, the whole SaveChanges fails. Then you have a huge context full of tracked entities and it may be annoying to identify and recover.

With chunks, you know the failure happened in a smaller group.
People chunk it by beginning a transaction, iterating rows.Chunk(1000), adding each chunk, SaveChanges, Clear, then committing.

For 10,000 rows, SaveChanges per row means roughly:
10,000 flushes
10,000 sets of command-building work
10,000 database round trips or batches
10,000 transactions if no outer transaction

Even inside one outer transaction, it is still usually slow.

Chunking gives a balance:
not one SaveChanges per row
not one massive SaveChanges for everything
one SaveChanges per chunk

Instead of:
100,000 rows -> 100,000 SaveChanges calls
or:
100,000 rows -> one giant SaveChanges call
you do:
100,000 rows -> 100 SaveChanges calls of 1,000 rows each

Why keep one outer transaction?

Because the business requirement may be:
import the whole file or import none of it

But technically you cannot comfortably track/save 500,000 entities at once.

So you get:
one business transaction
many EF persistence batches

This is also where automatic savepoints may create overhead: every chunk's SaveChanges creates a savepoint if AutoSavepointsEnabled is true inside a manually-started transaction.

theme: Multiple SaveChanges reduces memory is incomplete
text: If someone says: "Multiple SaveChanges() reduces memory" — that is incomplete.

theme: Real pattern: SaveChanges plus Clear or fresh context
text:
The real pattern is:
foreach chunk:
  AddRange(chunk)
  SaveChangesAsync()
  ChangeTracker.Clear()

or:
foreach chunk:
  create a fresh DbContext
  AddRange(chunk)
  SaveChangesAsync()

SaveChanges alone does not detach tracked entities.

If the whole bulk import is inside one long outer transaction, chunked SaveChanges is not mainly a lock-release optimization. Chunked saves inside one long transaction may acquire locks earlier:
one huge SaveChanges near the end: locks are acquired when the big save starts
chunked SaveChanges from the beginning: chunk 1 locks may be acquired early and held until final commit

So the lock objection is valid.

theme: Flush one phase before another phase
text:
3. You want to flush one phase before another phase

Example:
Begin transaction.
Phase 1: create order; SaveChanges.
Phase 2: reserve inventory; SaveChanges.
Phase 3: write audit; SaveChanges.
Commit.

This pattern flushes phase outputs before later phases run.

theme: ChangeTracker.Clear docs and short-lived DbContext preference
text: EF Core docs say ChangeTracker.Clear() clears all tracked entities and is more efficient than detaching entities one by one. They also describe the recommended DbContext lifetime as short-lived: create the context, track entities, call SaveChanges, then dispose it.

So the memory benefit comes from:
SaveChanges + ChangeTracker.Clear()
or:
SaveChanges + dispose DbContext
not from SaveChanges() alone.

ChangeTracker.Clear() is a big hammer.

It clears everything currently tracked by that DbContext, not just the entities from the latest chunk.

Rule:
Use Clear() when the DbContext is only being used for temporary batch tracking.
Avoid Clear() when the same DbContext is also tracking important entities you still plan to update, save, inspect, or use for relationship fix-up.

In normal business code, prefer a short-lived DbContext and let disposal clean it up. Use Clear deliberately in bulk/import loops where you know exactly what is being tracked.

There is a tradeoff, but in most apps allocating a DbContext per chunk is not a big problem. A DbContext is designed to be short-lived and is not supposed to be a long-lived heavyweight object. The expensive things are usually not allocating the DbContext; the expensive things are database round trips, SQL execution, change tracking thousands of entities, large object graphs, transaction/log/lock work, and network latency.

theme: Clear can accidentally detach important tracked entities
text:
Dangerous Clear example: load customer, set LastImportStartedAt, later bulk import chunks with AddRange/SaveChanges/Clear. Clear also detaches customer. A later SaveChanges may not save customer changes because customer is no longer tracked.

After Clear(), customer is just a normal C# object. EF is no longer tracking its change.

theme: Multiple saves because phases depend on previous writes
text: A workflow might be written as multiple saves because each phase depends on the previous one being flushed to the database, because of triggers, computed columns, constraints, generated values, raw SQL, stored procedures, or queries that need to see the previous writes.

theme: Preference: dedicated context or separate contexts
text:
Preference:
For simple bulk import code:
one dedicated context + SaveChanges + Clear

For complex business workflows:
separate contexts for separate phases

For evolving codebases where bugs from Clear would be expensive, a fresh context per chunk is often worth the tiny allocation cost.

Avoid one giant SaveChanges pipeline

SaveChanges() has to detect changes before saving. EF Core docs say change detection happens when SaveChanges is called to ensure changed values are detected before sending updates to the database.

If one context tracks 300,000 entities, SaveChanges has a large amount of work to process in one go. Chunking keeps each flush smaller.

4. You want partial rollback inside the transaction

This is where manual savepoints make sense.

Example: phase 1 is mandatory, phase 2 is optional.
Begin transaction, add order, SaveChanges, create savepoint AfterOrder, try add discount and SaveChanges; on failure rollback to savepoint and continue without discount.
Safer pattern: use a separate context for the bulk work. The main context tracks the import job and saves its state; a bulk context handles the large batch.
Another safe pattern is a fresh context per chunk. Then you do not need Clear() because disposing the context removes all tracking for that chunk.

theme: Do not roll back whole transaction for optional part
text: Continuation of partial rollback workflow: after optional discount handling, add an audit log, SaveChanges, commit. Here you do not want to roll back the whole transaction; you only want to undo one part.

theme: Bulk context chunking then update import job
text: Continuation of separate context pattern: bulkContext imports chunks with AddRange/SaveChanges/Clear; mainContext then marks the import job completed and saves it.

Why disable automatic savepoints?

Usually you do not disable them. You disable automatic savepoints only when you intentionally decide:
I do not want EF to create a savepoint before every SaveChanges.
I will decide where savepoints are needed.

theme: Separate contexts protect main tracked entity
text:
Here:
mainContext tracks the import job
bulkContext tracks only chunk entities
bulkContext.Clear() cannot accidentally detach the import job
